chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
“You shouldn't sell in winter.” Really? In Quebec, winter has its particularities — snow, cold, short days — but it also offers real opportunities, both for buying and selling. This guide separates myth from reality, season by season.

You'll see why winter buyers are often the most serious, how to present a property when everything is white, what advantages winter gives the buyer, and how to handle the practical aspects specific to the Quebec climate (snow removal, inspection under the snow, moving at -20°C).

Each chapter ends with a concrete tip. At the end, an action plan, a glossary and a quiz to anchor the essentials.

This guide's benchmarks apply to Greater Montréal: adapt them to your area and always validate your strategy with your broker according to market conditions at the time of acting.

chapters.title: The myth of the “wrong season”
chapters.html:
Nuancing a stubborn preconception.

There are generally fewer properties for sale and fewer buyers in winter. But “fewer” doesn't mean “bad”: it's often the opposite for those who know how to read the market.

The buyers who visit in January at -15°C aren't Sunday tourists: they have a real need (a job transfer, a separation, a growing family, a lease ending) and a tight schedule. On the other side, fewer sellers list, so your property faces less direct competition than at the height of spring.

What the season really changes:

  • Volume: fewer listings and fewer active buyers.
  • Motivation: the buyers present are more decided.
  • Competition: fewer comparable properties listed at the same time as yours.
  • Timelines: sometimes a bit longer, but with firmer offers.

Result: a good property, well prepared and above all well priced, can sell very well in winter — sometimes faster than an overpriced one drowned in the spring supply.

Emilie's tip

Don't postpone a sale just “because it's winter”. A buyer who comes out in a storm is a motivated buyer. Fewer visitors, but a far higher rate of seriousness: it's often a winning trade-off for the seller.

chapters.title: Selling in winter: presenting well
chapters.objective: Offsetting the season's challenges, point by point.
chapters.html:
Offsetting the season's challenges, point by point.

Winter calls for a few presentation adjustments, all easy to master once you think of them. The goal: that the buyer forgets the cold the moment they step through the door.

Outside, the first impression plays out even before the entrance:

  • Clear snow and ice from the entrance, the steps and the sidewalk before every visit — it's a matter of welcome and safety (liability).
  • Clear the address plate, the porch and access to the shed or garage.
  • Provide an absorbent mat and a space for boots at the entrance.

Inside, you sell comfort and warmth:

  • Maximize the light (short days): curtains open, all the lamps on, warm-light bulbs.
  • Heat to a welcoming temperature during visits.
  • Showcase the energy efficiency: recent windows, insulation, a heat pump, a fireplace.

Finally, offset the absence of greenery: add to the file a few summer photos of the lot, the yard and the landscaping, so the buyer sees the property's full potential.

Emilie's tip

In winter, sell a feeling: a warm, bright home that's easy to access despite the snow. And always show what the lot looks like in summer — that's what the buyer can't imagine under 40 cm of snow.

chapters.title: Buying in winter: opportunities
chapters.objective: Taking advantage on the buyer's side.
chapters.html:
Taking advantage on the buyer's side.

For the buyer, winter is often the best season — provided you know how to look. Two advantages combine: less competition and an inspection “in extreme conditions”.

Less competition, more power. With few active buyers, bidding wars are rarer and the sellers present are often in a hurry (a move already planned, a property already vacant, a double mortgage to avoid). Your room to negotiate widens.

The house shows its true colours. The cold reveals what summer hides. Use the visit to observe:

  • Drafts at the windows and doors, a “cold wall” sensation.
  • The efficiency and noise of the heating; ask for the real costs of the last 12 months.
  • The presence of ice on the ground, ice dams on the roof or abundant icicles (a sign of deficient insulation or attic ventilation).
  • The quality of the snow removal and access; how a sloped driveway behaves.

You thus test the property in its most demanding conditions — an inspection advantage the summer buyer will never have.

Emilie's tip

Buying in winter means seeing the house at its worst: drafts, ice, the real heating bill. What you observe in January won't surprise you the following winter — and it gives you concrete arguments to negotiate.

chapters.title: Each season has its logic
chapters.objective: Choosing the timing by your priorities, not by prejudice.
chapters.html:
Choosing the timing by your priorities, not by prejudice.

Rather than a “good” or “bad” season, think in terms of trade-offs. Each period has its strengths and weaknesses, for the buyer as for the seller.

  • Spring: the most active market. Lots of choice and buyers, clear lots — but strong competition and frequent bidding wars.
  • Summer: a sustained market, exteriors and pools at their best; a slowdown during the construction holiday.
  • Fall: serious buyers who want to settle in before winter; a short window before the slowdown.
  • Winter: less volume, but reduced competition and highly motivated buyers.

The “best” moment therefore depends on your goal: maximizing the number of buyers (spring), reducing competition (winter), or simply following your life calendar (a transfer, a birth, retirement). A seller who wants little competition and a buyer who wants to negotiate can both do very well in January.

In every case, price and preparation weigh far more than the season. A well-priced, impeccable property sells in any season; an overpriced one lingers even in spring.

Emilie's tip

Don't let the calendar decide for you. The real question isn't “is it the right season?” but “is it the right time for me, and is my price fair?” Those two answers count far more than the weather.

chapters.title: Practical aspects of the Quebec winter
chapters.objective: Anticipating the logistics specific to the climate.
chapters.html:
Anticipating the logistics specific to the climate.

In Quebec, winter adds concrete realities to the transaction. Well anticipated, they become simple organization rather than nasty surprises.

Inspection. Snow can hide the roof, the slope of the lot, the drainage, a slab crack or the state of the cladding. Ask the seller for summer photos, note these points at the inspection and, if needed, plan an additional check at the thaw.

Moving. Icy roads, short days and sub-zero temperatures complicate the logistics:

  • Book early: good movers get scarce and July 1 isn't the only possible date.
  • Protect floors and furniture from road salt and moisture (mats, reinforced boxes).
  • Keep a margin in the schedule in case of a storm.

Taking possession. As soon as you get the keys, check that the heating works, that the water hasn't been shut off (risk of frozen pipes in a vacant unit) and that the access is cleared. Finally, make sure your home insurance is in force before the deep cold, including for a temporarily unoccupied property.

Emilie's tip

You don't buy what you can't see. If the snow hides the roof and the lot, require summer photos and have it recorded at the inspection. And for any home left empty in winter: heating kept on and water monitored, otherwise a frozen pipe can cost a fortune.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Decide my strategy without a seasonal bias.
  2. List the winter adjustments (snow removal, light).

Within 30 days

  1. Prepare a warm, accessible presentation.
  2. Take advantage of a less crowded market.

Next

  1. Act according to my needs, not the calendar.

Depending on the season

  1. Adapt my presentation (snow removal, light, warmth) if I sell in winter.
  2. Take advantage of reduced competition and test the house in deep cold if I buy in winter.

  • Winter curb appeal: cleared access and a warm presentation.
  • Winter test: observing insulation, heating and infiltration in deep cold.
  • Seller competition: lower in winter.
  • Seasonality: the variation in market activity by season.

  • Winter test: observing insulation, heating and infiltration in deep cold.
  • Ice dam: a buildup of ice at the roof's edge, a sign of insulation/ventilation to check.
  • Winter possession: check heating, water and access as soon as you get the keys.
